claim: Entorhinal grid cells implement a spatial code with hexagonal periodicity.
source: Entorhinal grid cells implement a spatial code with hexagonal periodicity, signaling the position of the animal within an environment.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Grid maps of cells belonging to the same module share spacing and orientation.
source: Grid maps of cells belonging to the same module share spacing and orientation, only differing in relative two-dimensional spatial phase, which could result from being part of a two-dimensional attractor guided by path integration.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: A simpler one-dimensional attractor is enough to align grid cells equally well as a two-dimensional attractor.
source: Here, we show that a simpler one-dimensional attractor is enough to align grid cells equally well.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by simulation data comparing 1D and 2D attractors.

claim: The resulting population activity from a one-dimensional attractor is a sample of a torus.
source: Using topological data analysis, we show that the resulting population activity is a sample of a torus, while the ensemble of maps preserves features of the network architecture.
evidence: This is demonstrated through topological data analysis methods applied to simulation data.

claim: The flexibility of a low dimensional attractor allows it to negotiate the geometry of the representation manifold with the feedforward inputs.
source: The flexibility of this low dimensional attractor allows it to negotiate the geometry of the representation manifold with the feedforward inputs, rather than imposing it.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results showing different configuration orders in Figure 6.

claim: The architecture and the representation manifold of an attractor need not be topological objects of the same dimensionality.
source: More generally, our results represent a proof of principle against the intuition that the architecture and the representation manifold of an attractor are topological objects of the same dimensionality, with implications to the study of attractor networks across the brain.
evidence: This is demonstrated by showing that 1D and stripe attractors produce 2D toroidal population activity.

claim: Grid cells have been compared to a system of Cartesian axes.
source: Grid cells in the medial entorhinal cortex and other brain areas provide a representation of the spatial environment navigated by an animal, through maps of hexagonal periodicity that have been compared to a system of Cartesian axes (Moser et al., 2008; Fyhn et al., 2004; Buzsáki and Moser, 2013).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The alignment of axes of symmetry between neighboring, co-modular neurons in most computational models occurs through local synaptic interactions.
source: While different mechanisms have been proposed as the basis to make a neuron develop a collection of responsive fields distributed in space with hexagonal periodicity, the alignment of axes of symmetry between neighboring, co-modular neurons in most computational models occurs through local synaptic interactions between them (Kropff and Treves, 2008; Couey et al., 2013; Burak and Fiete, 2009; Burgess et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to previous modeling work.

claim: The network responsible for grid cell alignment can be thought of as a two-dimensional continuous attractor.
source: In general, the network responsible for this communication can be thought of as a two-dimensional continuous attractor (Knierim and Zhang, 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a general understanding in the field with a supporting citation.

claim: Grid cells are capable of representing one dimensional variables such as space, time or the frequency of a sound.
source: First, grid cells are also capable of representing one dimensional variables such as space, time or the frequency of a sound, or three-dimensional space, exhibiting poor to no periodicity (Aronov et al., 2017; Kraus et al., 2015; Yoon et al., 2016; Hafting et al., 2008; Grieves et al., 2021; Ginosar et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated with multiple supporting citations.

claim: Grid maps can suffer global or local modifications in response to different experimental manipulations.
source: Second, two-dimensional attractors impose a rather rigid constraint on the activity of neurons, but grid maps can suffer global or local modifications in response to different experimental manipulations (Barry et al., 2007; Yoon et al., 2013; Krupic et al., 2015; Krupic et al., 2018; Boccara et al., 2019; Butler et al., 2019; Sanguinetti-Scheck and Brecht, 2020).
evidence: This is stated with multiple supporting citations.

claim: When animals are trained to navigate deprived from sensory and vestibular feedback, entorhinal cells tend to develop a ring (1D) rather than toroidal (2D) population dynamic.
source: Fourth, a recent experiment shows that when animals are trained to navigate deprived from sensory and vestibular feedback, entorhinal cells tend to develop a surprising ring (1D) rather than toroidal (2D) population dynamic (Gonzalo Cogno et al., 2024).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to experimental work.

claim: The model includes 225 input cells and 100 grid cells.
source: We performed 100 simulations of a simplified version of this self-organizing network (Methods), including 225 input cells and NEC = 100 grid cells, in two otherwise identical setups.
evidence: This is a direct description of the model parameters used in the simulations.

claim: Maps in both 2D and 1D simulations had hexagonal symmetry at the end of the learning process.
source: At the end of the learning process, maps in both types of simulation had hexagonal symmetry (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The mean population autocorrelogram had hexagonal symmetry, indicating that individual maps within the network shared spacing and orientation.
source: The mean population autocorrelogram also had hexagonal symmetry, indicating that individual maps within the network shared spacing and orientation (Figure 1d), which was further confirmed by the clustering into six well-defined groups of first-order autocorrelogram maxima for the pool of all cells (Figure 1e), with phases were distributed in distinctive patterns for both conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figures 1d and 1e.

claim: Gridness was highest for 1D, followed closely by 2D and 1DL, while the No condition exhibited markedly lower values.
source: Gridness was highest for 1D, followed closely by 2D and 1 DL, while the No condition exhibited markedly lower values.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Spacing and spread were lowest for the 2D condition, followed by a small margin by 1D and 1DL, with the No condition presenting the largest differences.
source: Spacing and spread were lowest for the 2D condition, followed by a small margin by 1D and 1 DL, with the No condition again presenting the largest differences with the rest.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Attractor connectivity of all investigated types not only aligns grid cells similarly but also has the effect of compressing maps in terms of spacing.
source: These results suggest that attractor connectivity of all investigated types not only aligns grid cells similarly but also has the effect of compressing maps in terms of spacing.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing lower spacing in conditions with attractors.

claim: Individual spacing negatively correlates with time for the 2D (R: –0.78, p: 10–84), 1D (R: –0.77, p: 10–79), and 1DL (R: –0.74, p: 10–71) conditions.
source: Individual spacing negatively correlates with time for the 2D (R: –0.78, p: 10–84), 1D (R: –0.77, p: 10–79), and 1 DL (R: –0.74, p: 10–71).
evidence: This is stated with specific correlation values and p-values from the data analysis.

claim: A combination of progressive increase in gridness and decrease in spacing across days has been observed in animals familiarizing with a novel environment.
source: A combination of progressive increase in gridness and decrease in spacing across days has been observed in animals familiarizing with a novel environment (Barry et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to experimental work.

claim: In all conditions with attractors, most of the data points had a local dimensionality equal to 2 (more than 90%).
source: In all conditions, most of the data points had a local dimensionality equal to 2 (more than 90% in all conditions), with eventual outliers that had some impact on the mean but not on the median (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The population activity in all conditions with attractors is concentrated around a structure with a local dimension of 2.
source: These results suggest that the population activity in all conditions with attractors is concentrated around a structure with a local dimension of 2.
evidence: This is inferred from the local dimensionality analysis results.

claim: Most of the data points had β1=1, which was the case for more than 90% of data in conditions with attractors and around 70% in the No condition.
source: We observed that most of the data points had β1=1, which was the case for more than 90% of data in conditions with attractors and around 70% in the No condition.
evidence: This is stated based on the local homology analysis.

claim: The population activity for simulations with attractors is locally two-dimensional, without boundary or singularities, forming a closed surface.
source: Put together, these results suggest that the population activity for simulations with attractors is locally two-dimensional, without boundary or singularities, forming a closed surface.
evidence: This is inferred from the local dimensionality and local homology analyses.

claim: Data clouds in the No condition do not meet the first two conditions of the theorem of classification of closed surfaces.
source: In contrast, data clouds in the No condition do not meet the first two conditions of the theorem of classification of closed surfaces, and are compatible with a two-dimensional sheet exhibiting a boundary along the edge of the space selected for analysis.
evidence: This is inferred from the local dimensionality and local homology analyses showing boundaries.

claim: The population activity in all cases with attractors is an orientable manifold.
source: The pooled distribution of such diagrams and the averages across 100 simulations of each type (Methods) were almost identical for conditions 1D, 2D (Figure 4a and b) and 1 DL (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), indicating that the population activity in all cases is an orientable manifold.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing persistence diagrams in Z2 and Z3.

claim: From the average diagrams for all conditions with attractors, Betti numbers could be qualitatively estimated as those of a torus: β0=1, β1=2 and β2=1.
source: From the average diagrams for all conditions with attractors, Betti numbers could be qualitatively estimated as those of a torus: β0=1, β1=2 and β2=1 (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is stated based on the persistence diagram analysis shown in Figure 4a.

claim: 82 out of 100 simulations were classified as [1, 2, 1] in the 1D condition and 76 in the 2D condition.
source: When quantifying the Betti numbers for individual simulations using a common cutoff value (Methods), 82 (out of 100) were classified as [1, 2, 1] in the 1D condition and 76 in the 2D condition (Figure 4d), with small deviations compatible with a noisy scenario for the rest of the simulations.
evidence: This is stated with specific counts from the data analysis shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Different attractor architectures (torus, ring, stripe) similarly constrain the population activity into a torus embedded in a high dimensional space.
source: In summary, our analyses show that different attractor architectures (torus, ring, stripe) similarly constrain the population activity into a torus embedded in a high dimensional space.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the topological analysis of population activity.

claim: For the 2D condition, only 27 simulations had Betti numbers [1,2,1], while 69 had Betti numbers [1,2,0] where the cavity could not be correctly identified.
source: However, in individual persistence diagrams only 27 simulations had Betti numbers [1,2,1], while 69 had Betti numbers [1,2,0] where the cavity could not be correctly identified (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is stated with specific counts from the analysis of the transpose matrix shown in Figure 5c.

claim: 86% of 1D simulations had Betti numbers of a ring [1,1,0].
source: In contrast, 1D simulations had an average persistence diagram similar to the majority of individual diagrams (86%), characterized by the Betti numbers of a ring [1,1,0], while for 1 DL simulations the average diagram and 97% of individual diagrams had Betti numbers [1,0,0] compatible with a stripe.
evidence: This is stated with specific percentages from the analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: 97% of 1DL simulations had Betti numbers [1,0,0] compatible with a stripe.
source: In contrast, 1D simulations had an average persistence diagram similar to the majority of individual diagrams (86%), characterized by the Betti numbers of a ring [1,1,0], while for 1 DL simulations the average diagram and 97% of individual diagrams had Betti numbers [1,0,0] compatible with a stripe.
evidence: This is stated with specific percentages from the analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The analysis on the matrix M showed that all conditions with attractors had a population activity embedded in a torus, while the analysis on its transpose showed qualitative differences across conditions.
source: In summary, the analysis on the matrix M showed that all conditions with attractors had a population activity embedded in a torus, while the analysis on its transpose showed qualitative differences across conditions, where in general the homology recapitulated that of the architecture of recurrent connections.
evidence: This is the summary conclusion from comparing the two types of topological analyses.

claim: The geometry of the attractor layout in physical space allowed for a classification into 4 orders (O0 to O3) with different prevalence.
source: While all individual colors in these maps had hexagonal periodicity, as expected from a population of aligned grid maps, the geometry of the attractor layout in physical space allowed for a classification into 4 orders (O0 to O3) with different prevalence (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is stated based on the analysis of population maps shown in Figure 6.

claim: The constraint imposed by hexagonal symmetry is compatible with a countably infinite number of configurations.
source: This conceptualization implies that, although we only found 4 configurations for aligning grid cells with a 1D attractor, the constraint imposed by hexagonal symmetry is compatible with a countably infinite number of them (as many as orders of neighbors in a hexagonal grid), provided attractors are able to stretch enough in physical space.
evidence: This is inferred from the mathematical properties of hexagonal grids and the observed configurations.

claim: The weak constraint imposed by one-dimensional flexible attractors allows for many possible solutions to co-exist as local minima of the self-organization energy landscape.
source: These results show that the weak constraint imposed by one-dimensional flexible attractors allows for many possible solutions to co-exist as local minima of the self-organization energy landscape.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of multiple configuration orders in the simulations.

claim: Three-dimensional Isomap projections allowed for the visualization of the twisted torus in all conditions with attractors.
source: For our data, three-dimensional Isomap projections (Tenenbaum et al., 2000) allowed for the visualization of the twisted torus in all conditions with attractors.
evidence: This is stated based on the dimensionality reduction analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The same Isomap procedure produced different visualizations (tetrahedron or torus-like shapes) for different simulations.
source: Other times the same reduction technique, with identical parameters, produced directly a torus-like shape, squeezed at two opposite sides (Figure 7b and c). While extreme solutions looked like the tetrahedron or the torus, intermediate visualizations were also found which could not be clearly interpreted as one or the other.
evidence: This is stated based on the observations from Figure 7.

claim: If the attractor is inactive, weak or shuffled, grid maps exhibit markedly lower levels of hexagonal symmetry and do not align.
source: Crucially, if the attractor is inactive, weak or shuffled, grid maps obtained under otherwise identical conditions exhibit markedly lower levels of hexagonal symmetry and do not align, failing to constrain the population activity into a torus.
evidence: This is stated based on the results shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Grid cells represent multiple geometries with individual characteristics in each case.
source: Grid cells, for example, represent multiple geometries with individual characteristics in each case.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the discussion.

claim: In one- and three-dimensional spatial tasks grid cells exhibit multiple fields with larger and more irregular spacing than in two-dimensional navigation.
source: In one- and three-dimensional spatial tasks grid cells exhibit multiple fields, as in two-dimensional navigation, but with larger and more irregular spacing (Yoon et al., 2016; Hafting et al., 2008; Grieves et al., 2021; Ginosar et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: In one-dimensional tasks involving the representation of frequency of a sound or time, grid cells much more often develop single response fields.
source: In other one-dimensional tasks, involving the representation of frequency of a sound or time, they much more often develop single response fields (Aronov et al., 2017; Kraus et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: One-dimensional attractors are simple enough to emerge independently of experience, as exhibited by head direction cells in rats prior to eye-opening.
source: One-dimensional attractors are simple enough to emerge independently of experience, as exhibited by head direction cells in rats prior to eye-opening (Bjerknes et al., 2015) or internally generated sequences in the hippocampus (Pastalkova et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Experiments in which animals navigate in the dark support path integration functionality for hippocampal and entorhinal maps.
source: Experiments in which animals navigate in the dark support this functionality for hippocampal and entorhinal maps, and it has been recently shown that the path integrator can be recalibrated in an almost online fashion (Jayakumar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The involvement of some or all grid cells in path integration still needs to find direct experimental proof.
source: However, although from a theoretical perspective grid cells are ideal candidates to implement path integration, the involvement of some or all grid cells in this operation still needs to find direct experimental proof.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Grid cells were originally described in superficial layers of the medial entorhinal cortex, but were later found also in other entorhinal layers and in an increasing number of other brain areas.
source: Grid cells were originally described in superficial layers of the medial entorhinal cortex, but were later found also in other entorhinal layers and even in an increasing number of other brain areas (Boccara et al., 2010; Long et al., 2021a; Long and Zhang, 2021b).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Grid cell properties change substantially during the early life of rodents.
source: In addition, given that grid cell properties change substantially during the early life of rodents (Langston et al., 2010; Wills et al., 2010), flexible attractors could also be taken into account as a potential intermediate stage toward the formation of more complex architectures.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The model uses place cell-like inputs with Gaussian response fields with a standard deviation of 5.4 cm.
source: While the model works with arbitrary spatially stable inputs (Kropff and Treves, 2008), for simplicity we use place cell like inputs. Input cells had Gaussian response fields with a standard deviation of 5.4 cm centered at preferred positions uniformly distributed across the 1 m arena.
evidence: This is a direct description of the model implementation.

claim: The feedforward synaptic weight matrix is equipped with Hebbian plasticity.
source: The feedforward synaptic weight matrix WI is equipped with Hebbian plasticity, while for the purposes of this paper the recurrent synaptic weigh WEC is fixed (see next section).
evidence: This is a direct description of the model implementation.

claim: The recurrent synaptic weight is fixed in the model.
source: The feedforward synaptic weight matrix WI is equipped with Hebbian plasticity, while for the purposes of this paper the recurrent synaptic weigh WEC is fixed (see next section).
evidence: This is a direct description of the model implementation.

claim: For the 2D architecture, the strength of connectivity between a given pair of cells was set to depend on their relative position through a function defined as the sum of three cosine functions in directions 120° apart.
source: The strength of connectivity between a given pair of cells k and l was set to depend on their relative position x = [xk - xl, yk - yl], through a function f(x) that was defined as the sum of three cosine functions in directions ki, 120° and 240° from each other, i.e. an ideal grid map (Kropff and Treves, 2008)
evidence: This is a direct description of the model implementation for the 2D architecture.

claim: For the 1D condition, neurons were uniformly distributed along an imaginary ring, spaced by 3.6°.
source: For the 1D condition, neurons were uniformly distributed along an imaginary ring, spaced by 3.6°. The connection strength between any pair of neurons was defined as proportional to a 7.2° standard deviation Gaussian function of the minimum angle between them.
evidence: This is a direct description of the model implementation for the 1D architecture.

claim: The kNN-distance was used as an estimator of the geodesic distance for studying the topology of the population activity.
source: For the purpose of capturing the intrinsic geometry of the underlying space determined by these point clouds, and to avoid the effects of the 'curse of dimensionality', we endowed each point cloud with an estimator of the geodesic distance. This estimator, known as the kNN-distance, is defined as the length of the shortest path along the k-nearest neighbors graph, a graph with an edge between every data point and each of its k-nearest neighbors with respect to the ambient Euclidean distance.
evidence: This is a direct description of the analysis method.

claim: The value k=10 was set for all topological analyses of population activity.
source: We set the value k=10 for all our analyses but similar results could be obtained for a range of similar values of k.
evidence: This is a direct description of the analysis parameter.

claim: Persistent homology was computed to robustly recover geometric information such as the number of connected components, cycles and holes of different dimensions from the simulated data.
source: We aimed to robustly recover geometric information, such as the number of connected components, cycles and holes of different dimensions, from the simulated data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a). To do so, we computed the persistent homology Boissonnat et al., 2018; Edelsbrunner and Harer, 2008; Edelsbrunner et al., 2024; Zomorodian and Carlsson, 2005 of each point cloud endowed with its respective metric structure.
evidence: This is a direct description of the analysis method with supporting citations.

claim: Local neighborhoods of size k=70 were employed for all simulations of population activity with attractors and k=20 for the ones in the No condition for local PCA.
source: We employed local neighborhoods of size k=70 for all simulations of population activity with attractors and k=20 for the ones in the No condition. These values were determined as the center of a range of k values with stable outcomes.
evidence: This is a direct description of the analysis parameters.

claim: Isomap is a non-linear dimensionality reduction method that assumes the data is a sample of a low dimensional manifold embedded in a high dimensional Euclidean space.
source: Isomap is a celebrated (non-linear) dimensionality reduction method that assumes the data is a sample of a low dimensional manifold embedded in a high dimensional Euclidean space. It reduces the dimensionality by mapping the original data into a lower dimensional Euclidean space while preserving geodesic distances on the manifold subjacent in the data.
evidence: This is a description of the Isomap method.

claim: Dimensionality reduction procedures do not provide guarantee a priori to preserve the topology of the underlying manifold.
source: We remark that, even though dimensionality reduction procedures may serve as a useful tool for data visualization and feature extraction as part of a machine learning pipeline, they do not provide guarantee a priori to preserve the topology of the underlying manifold, so they do not constitute in general a proof of structure of the original data neither an accurate preprocessing method for a subsequent rigorous geometric analysis.
evidence: This is stated as a cautionary note about the limitations of dimensionality reduction methods.
